articles.title: Beyond surveillance: humanitarian lessons on integrating physical health into refugee health responses
articles.description: Agreement: I Agree Body: Dear Editor, The BMJ article by Touhid powerfully illustrates how dengue exposes the fragility of health systems serving displaced populations. While the immediate challenge is vector-borne disease, the wider lesson extends beyond Bangladesh. Humanitarian responses must resist separating infectious disease control from broader physical healthcare and communication support. During the UK Afghan resettlement programme following the fall of Kabul in 2021, we observed a similar principle in a very different setting. Although our role primarily focused on mental health and safeguarding assessments, many newly arrived families presented with untreated physical health needs that had remained unrecognised throughout displacement, including poorly controlled chronic diseases, dental pathology, anaemia, pregnancy-related complications, and unmet disability needs. These conditions were not unusual; they reflected disrupted healthcare access and the realities of forced migration. The Bangladesh experience highlights how infectious diseases flourish where health systems are overwhelmed, surveillance is incomplete, and displaced communities face barriers to care. Refugee camps in Cox's Bazar present obvious environmental risks for dengue transmission, but the exclusion of camp data from national surveillance also demonstrates how health inequalities can become statistically invisible. Similar invisibility occurs in high-income countries when refugee health is viewed solely through a mental health or safeguarding lens, while physical health needs rely on individuals successfully navigating unfamiliar healthcare systems. Communication is central to both contexts. Early recognition of deteriorating illness—whether dengue shock syndrome or pregnancy complications—depends on timely access to healthcare, professional interpretation, culturally appropriate health information, and trust in health services. These are not optional additions but core patient safety interventions. Delays in seeking care should not be understood simply as individual decisions but as consequences of structural, linguistic, and systemic barriers. Humanitarian medicine has long recognised that physical health, mental health, and social circumstances are inseparable. Initial health assessments routinely incorporate infectious disease, chronic illness, nutrition, pregnancy, disability, and psychosocial needs within a single framework. As global displacement increases and climate change alters the epidemiology of infectious diseases, this integrated approach becomes increasingly relevant beyond humanitarian settings. The authors rightly emphasise the interaction between climate change, displacement, and dengue. Health systems must now prepare not only for emerging infectious diseases but also for increasingly mobile populations whose healthcare has often been interrupted long before arrival. Strengthening surveillance is essential, but so too is ensuring that displaced populations receive holistic, accessible, and communication-aware healthcare from first contact. Bangladesh's experience reminds us that the consequences of delayed recognition are measured not only in epidemiological data, but also in preventable suffering and avoidable deaths. Humanitarian health responses offer valuable lessons for health systems worldwide: comprehensive screening, equitable communication, and integrated physical and mental healthcare should be regarded as fundamental components of preparedness rather than emergency measures.
